title: Cassowary

names.note: A separate headword from babarr 'older sister'. The two words sound the same.

identification.basis: The dictionary glosses kurranji simply as 'cassowary', and the southern cassowary is the only cassowary in Australia. Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service records the southern cassowary in Daintree National Park, on Eastern Kuku Yalanji country.

summary: **[Kurranji](word:kurranji)**, the southern cassowary (*Casuarius casuarius johnsonii*), is Australia's largest bird: up to 2 m tall and 76 kg, flightless, with a blue neck, red wattles and a horn-like casque on its head [ref:qld-cassowary]. Kuku Yalanji has its own words for a young cassowary, **[babarr](word:babarr)** and **[barbarr](word:barbarr)** [ref:hershberger1982]. Among the rainforest people of the lower Tully, south of Kuku Yalanji country, Roth saw cassowaries [speared](entry:spear-and-woomera) by hunters who imitated the bird's call, run down with dogs, and their chicks caught and raised in camp [ref:roth1901]. The bird is **Endangered** today [ref:qld-cassowary] [ref:ag-cassowary]. A cassowary has killed a person in Australia once on record, in 1926 [ref:kofron2003]. It is a rainforest bird: see each place for where it lives and where it does not.

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: The dictionary gives **[kurranji](word:kurranji)** for the cassowary, and two words for a young bird, **[babarr](word:babarr)** and **[barbarr](word:barbarr)** [ref:hershberger1982]. Babarr sounds the same as *[babarr](word:babarr)* 'older sister', but the dictionary lists the two as separate words [ref:hershberger1982]. Having its own names for the young bird fits a creature whose chicks look quite different from the adults. They are striped yellow and black at first, then turn brown before they grow into the black adult plumage [ref:am-cassowary].

sections.heading: Description
sections.body:
A huge, flightless bird, 1.5–2 m tall. Its body feathers are black, coarse and hair-like. The bare skin of the head and front of the neck is blue, the back of the neck is red, and two red wattles hang from the throat. On its head it carries a tall greyish casque, or helmet [ref:am-cassowary]. Queensland gives its weight as up to 76 kg [ref:qld-cassowary]. Females are bigger than males, with taller casques and brighter colours [ref:am-cassowary]. The innermost toe of each foot carries a long, very sharp claw [ref:am-cassowary]. That claw is the reason the bird is dangerous (see *Safety*).

Cassowaries usually live alone and keep to the same patch of forest all year [ref:am-cassowary]. They eat mostly fallen fruit: over 238 plant species, with some small animals, fungi and snails [ref:qld-cassowary]. Some rainforest fruits are so big that the cassowary is the only animal that can swallow them and carry their seeds away [ref:qpws-daintree].

sections.heading: Where it lives
sections.body: Cassowaries once lived in the rainforests from north of Townsville to Cape York. Today there are three populations, one in the Wet Tropics and two on Cape York [ref:qld-cassowary]. On Cape York, 'the southern population lives in the vine forests of the McIlwraith and Iron ranges and a northern population in the less extensive vine forests north of Shelburne Bay'; in the Wet Tropics 'cassowaries range from Cooktown to Paluma Range' [ref:qld-cassowary]. They live in tropical rainforest and also use [mangroves](entry:mangroves) and [melaleuca](entry:paperbark) swamps, sometimes walking into woodland [ref:ag-cassowary].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Cassowaries breed in the drier part of the year, from about May to November [ref:qld-cassowary]. The female lays 3–5 large green eggs on the forest floor and then leaves. The male sits on them for about 50 days [ref:qld-cassowary]. He then guards the striped chicks for up to nine months [ref:ag-cassowary]. During this time males are very aggressive [ref:am-cassowary], so the breeding season is when people most need to keep their distance. Because the birds live on fallen fruit, they follow the fruiting of the forest through the year [ref:qld-cassowary].

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
**Food.** Roth's detailed account of cassowary hunting comes from the lower Tully River, south of Kuku Yalanji country. There it was the only bird that was [speared](entry:spear-and-woomera) [ref:roth1901]. The cassowary is a big package of meat and fat, and the general Kuku Yalanji word *[minya](word:minya)* covers 'meat, eggs (protein food)' [ref:hershberger1982]. The sources do not describe how Kuku Yalanji people used cassowary bones.

**Raising chicks.** On the lower Tully, Roth saw young cassowaries caught and fed by the rainforest people. They grew up around the camp and followed the people from camp to camp [ref:roth1902].

sections.heading: How it was hunted and cooked
sections.body:
No published account describes cassowary hunting on the Bloomfield itself. The nearest detailed record is Roth's, from the **lower Tully River** rainforest people [ref:roth1901]:

1. **Learn the bird's path.** The cassowary walks the same way to water.
2. **Hide** behind a tree beside that path.
3. **Call it in** by imitating the cassowary's own call.
4. **[Spear it](entry:spear-and-woomera)** as it walks past to the water.
5. Alternatively, **hunt it with dogs**. Young birds are **run down** on foot.

For cooking, Roth describes the stone **[earth oven](entry:earth-oven)** used **on the Bloomfield** (Kuku Yalanji *[kurrma](word:kurrma)*; Roth wrote it *kurma*) for meat [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982]:

1. Heat a number of **[stones](entry:stone)** well in a fire.
2. Rake the stones and ashes aside and quickly **dig a hole** where the fire was.
3. Line the bottom with **leaves**, several kinds of [ginger](entry:wild-ginger).
4. Lay in the **pieces of meat**, packing the **hot stones and ashes** among them.
5. Cover with more leaves or [tea-tree (paperbark)](entry:paperbark) bark, then a **layer of earth and stones**, and leave it to bake.

On the lower Tully, big carcasses were first cut into pieces with the hooked spines of a **[lawyer cane](entry:lawyer-cane)**, worked like a cross-cut saw [ref:roth1901]. Smaller pieces could simply be roasted on and in the hot ashes (*[dindal](word:dindal)*, 'to roast on coals') [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
**Cassowaries can kill.** The innermost claw on each foot is long and very sharp [ref:am-cassowary]. One person has been killed by a cassowary in Australia, in 1926: see the eastern coast.

A review of 221 attacks in Queensland found 150 were on people, and 75% of those were by birds that people had fed. Victims were chased or charged in 71% of cases and kicked in 15% [ref:kofron2003]. Four of the eight people seriously hurt were crouching or lying on the ground [ref:kofron2003]. If you meet a cassowary:

- **Stay standing.** Don't crouch, because that brings your head and body within reach of its feet [ref:kofron2003].
- **Back off slowly** or put a tree between you and the bird, without turning your back [ref:kofron2003].
- **Keep children close** and dogs on a lead [ref:kofron2003] [ref:qld-cassowary].
- **Never feed a cassowary.** It is illegal, and fed birds become bold and dangerous [ref:qld-cassowary] [ref:kofron2003].
- Give **males with chicks** a very wide berth [ref:am-cassowary].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
The southern cassowary is listed as **Endangered** under the Commonwealth *EPBC Act* [ref:ag-cassowary] and as Endangered in Queensland [ref:qld-cassowary]. The main threats are cars, dogs, land clearing and fragmented forest, and cyclones that strip the fruit [ref:ag-cassowary]. Drivers in cassowary country, including the Daintree and Cape Tribulation roads, are asked to slow down [ref:qld-cassowary].

Section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* lets native title holders hunt, fish and gather for **personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs** without the licences other people need [ref:alrc-s211]. For everyone else, native wildlife is protected under Queensland's *Nature Conservation Act 1992*, and taking it needs a licence or permit [ref:qld-nca]. In practice, a cassowary is not a bird anyone else may touch. Native title holders' rights differ from place to place: see each place, ask the Traditional Owners first, and follow park rules.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: Useful words: *[kurranji](word:kurranji)* 'cassowary'; *[babarr](word:babarr)*, *[barbarr](word:barbarr)* 'young cassowary'; *[jabil](word:jabil)* 'kick'; *[kaya](word:kaya)* 'dog'; *[damal](word:damal)* '[to spear](entry:spear-and-woomera)'; *[minya](word:minya)* 'meat, eggs (protein food)'; *[kurrma](word:kurrma)* '[earth oven](entry:earth-oven)' [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: **The cassowary does not live on the Hann River.** The river runs through open 'stringybark, bloodwood, Moreton Bay ash and ironbark' country [ref:wp-hann], and the Atlas of Living Australia holds no cassowary record in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru [ref:ala-hann]. The nearest cassowaries are in the rainforest from Cooktown south, and in the vine forests of the McIlwraith and Iron ranges further up Cape York [ref:qld-cassowary].

sections.heading: The big bird here is the emu
sections.body: The great flightless bird of the Hann country is the **emu**, not the cassowary: the Atlas holds 106 emu records in the same box, from 1979 to 2025 [ref:ala-hann]. Kuku Thaypan Elders name it *Nhye raeel* or *Nhye areeba* and count it among their culturally significant species [ref:standley2019]. Roth saw emus hunted 'in the hinterland of Princess Charlotte Bay', the country the Hann drains to, where 'the hunter wears a collar-like head-dress — made of a thick sheaf of long grass doubled and tied behind — and holds some bushes in front of him' [ref:roth1901]. Standley names the emu among the 'significant totem species' of the sandridge country [ref:standley2019]; totems belong to their custodians and are not told here.

sections.heading: How people dealt with it here
sections.body: No published record links the cassowary to the Possum, Thaypan or Lama Lama peoples of the Hann [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]. The cassowary records in the general sections come from the rainforest coast.

locations.summary: The cassowary is not a bird of the upper Mitchell. Someone staying at [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) would have to travel back east into the rainforest to meet one [ref:ala].

sections.heading: Where it lives here
sections.body: The cassowary is a rainforest bird. It does not belong to the dry open woodland and river country inland around the Mitchell River near Mt Carbine. Atlas of Living Australia records cluster in the rainforest on the ranges east of Mt Carbine, and there are almost none from the Mitchell River country to the west [ref:ala]. Someone staying at [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) would have to travel back east into the rainforest to meet one.

locations.summary: This is cassowary country: the rainforest from the Daintree to the Bloomfield [ref:qpws-daintree]. Roth's Bloomfield notes record fly-flicks of its feathers [ref:roth1904], and the only recorded human death from a cassowary in Australia was near Mossman in 1926 [ref:kofron2003].

sections.heading: Where it lives here
sections.body: On Eastern Kuku Yalanji country they live in the rainforest of the Daintree and Cape Tribulation coast [ref:qpws-daintree] and the ranges and lowlands between the Mossman, Daintree and Bloomfield rivers.

sections.heading: Feathers
sections.body: **Feathers.** Roth's Bloomfield River notes record fly-flicks made of cassowary feathers. They were made to the same design as the emu-feather flicks of Cape Bedford and the Palmer River: a bunch of quills bound onto a short handle, with the binding strengthened with gum cement [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: The 1926 death
sections.body: The only recorded human death from a cassowary in Australia happened on this country, near Mossman. On 6 April 1926 two boys and their dogs attacked a cassowary and tried to kill it. The older boy, 16, tripped and fell, and the bird jumped on him. Its claw went into his neck and cut a blood vessel, and he bled to death [ref:kofron2003].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: In September 2021 the Daintree, Ngalba Bulal, Kalkajaka and Hope Islands national parks, more than 160,000 ha between the Daintree and Cooktown, were handed back to the Eastern Kuku Yalanji people as Aboriginal land. They are jointly managed with the Queensland Government until Traditional Owners take over sole management [ref:handback2021]. The 2007 Eastern Kuku Yalanji native title determination recognises rights to hunt animals on the determination area, but not for trade or commerce [ref:walker2007]. Under Eastern Kuku Yalanji law (Ngujakura), the right to give permission to come onto country belongs to the Traditional Owners [ref:walker2007]. Visitors should ask first, and should follow park rules.
